components.note: 目 (eye) — 眼 refers directly to the eye itself.
艮 (gèn) gives a sound hint — 眼 is pronounced yǎn; the rhyme has drifted apart over the centuries.
目 (eye) — 睛 names the eyeball, part of the eye.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 睛.

example.hanzi: 她的眼睛很漂亮。
example.pinyin: Tā de yǎnjing hěn piàoliang.
example.english: Her eyes are very pretty.
example.fact: 睛 (the "eyeball" half of the compound) almost never appears on its own — outside 眼睛 and a few technical terms it's a bound morpheme that needs 眼 to form a usable word, while 眼 alone works fine by itself in compounds like 眼镜 ("glasses") and 眼泪 ("tears").

meanings: outside (also pr. [wai4 mian5] for this sense)

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — divination was traditionally done in the evening.
卜 (to divine, reading cracks in bone or shell) — combined with 夕 (evening), an evening divination was for unusual or 'outside' matters, giving 外 its meaning of 'outside' or 'foreign.'
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 外面在下雨,你要带伞。
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn zài xiàyǔ, nǐ yào dài sǎn.
example.english: It's raining outside, you should bring an umbrella.
example.fact: 外面 and its near-synonym 外边 both mean "outside" — paralleling the 这里/这儿 split for "here" — 外面 leans slightly more standard and written, 外边 slightly more colloquial and Beijing-flavored, though both are heard nationwide.

components.note: 囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 中国是一个历史悠久的国家。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó shì yí gè lìshǐ yōujiǔ de guójiā.
example.english: China is a country with a long history.
example.fact: 国家 literally combines 国 ("state") with 家 ("family, home") — a pairing that echoes classical Confucian political thought, which often pictured the state as an extension of the family, with the ruler cast as a kind of father figure over the realm.

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 这个蛋糕看上去很好吃。
example.pinyin: Zhège dàngāo kàn shàng qù hěn hǎochī.
example.english: This cake looks delicious.
example.fact: 看上去 is nearly interchangeable with 看起来 — both mean "it appears, it seems" and are built the same way: verb 看 plus a directional complement (上去 "up and away" vs 起来 "up") that has faded into pure grammatical function and no longer describes literal direction.

components.note: 口 (mouths) — 总 pictures many voices.
心 (heart, mind) — many mouths brought together under one mind gave 总 its meaning 'overall' or 'to gather together.'
纟 (thread) — 统 relates to threads gathered into one continuous strand, extending to the idea of unifying or governing as one system.
充 (chōng) gives a hint of the sound — 统 is pronounced tǒng, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 美国总统住在白宫。
example.pinyin: Měiguó zǒngtǒng zhù zài Báigōng.
example.english: The US president lives in the White House.
example.fact: 总统 is reserved for the head of a republic — translating "president" as in the US or France — while China's own head of state carries the separate title 主席 ("chairman"), so 总统 essentially never refers to a Chinese leader.

example.hanzi: 他的话深深伤害了她。
example.pinyin: Tā de huà shēnshēn shānghài le tā.
example.english: His words deeply hurt her.
example.fact: 伤害 is transitive — it needs an object, someone or something being harmed (伤害她, "hurt her") — while its near-relative 受伤 ("to get injured," literally "receive injury") is intransitive and describes the person harmed, a transitivity contrast that trips up many learners translating English "hurt" and "injured."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 控 relates to controlling or restraining something by hand
空 (kōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 控's reading kòng
刂 (knife) — 制 relates to cutting and shaping, and by extension, to making or controlling something.
巾 (jīn) gives a hint of the sound — 制 is pronounced zhì, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 她很难控制自己的情绪。
example.pinyin: Tā hěn nán kòngzhì zìjǐ de qíngxù.
example.english: She finds it hard to control her emotions.
example.fact: 控 (built from 扌 "hand") contributes a sense of restraining or holding back, while 制 (built from 刂 "knife") contributes a sense of cutting, shaping, or regulating — together 控制 layers "restrain" onto "regulate" for its modern sense of control.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 最 pictures something happening under the sun, that is, everywhere.
取 (to take, gather) — combined with the sun above, gathering everything under the sun gave 最 its meaning of 'most' or 'the utmost.'
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 近's meaning 'near, close,' a short distance to walk.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound hint — 近 is pronounced jìn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 你最近怎么样?
example.pinyin: Nǐ zuìjìn zěnmeyàng?
example.english: How have you been recently?
example.fact: Unlike English "recently," which points only to the past, 最近 can describe the near future too (最近可能会下雨, "it may rain in the next while") — its literal meaning is just "nearest [in time]," and context decides which direction from now it points.

components.note: 声 (simplified from 聲) refers to sound; the traditional form combined several elements related to hearing and music, simplified here into a more compact shape.
立 here depicts a tongue positioned to speak.
日 here depicts an open mouth — a tongue forming sound in the mouth gave 音 its meaning 'sound, tone.'

example.hanzi: 我喜欢她说话的声音。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan tā shuōhuà de shēngyīn.
example.english: I like the sound of her voice.
example.fact: Like 喜欢 in the companion character-deck's pilot batch, 声音 pairs two already near-synonymous roots — 声 ("sound, voice," as in 大声 "loudly") and 音 ("sound, tone," as in 音乐 "music") — reinforcing each other into one common noun.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'
乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'

example.hanzi: 祝你生日快乐!
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ shēngrì kuàilè!
example.english: Happy birthday to you!
example.fact: 快乐 tends to describe a lasting state of happiness or well-being — it's the word behind nearly every Chinese festival greeting (生日快乐 "happy birthday," 新年快乐 "happy new year") — while 高兴 describes a more momentary feeling of being pleased about something happening right now.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'

example.hanzi: 这只小猫真可爱。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī xiǎomāo zhēn kě'ài.
example.english: This kitten is really cute.
example.fact: 可爱 follows a productive pattern where 可 ("able to be, worthy of") attaches to a verb to form an adjective — the same template builds 可怕 ("worthy of fear" → "scary") and 可惜 ("worthy of pity" → "a pity, unfortunately"), so spotting 可+verb is a shortcut to guessing a whole family of adjectives.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.
入 depicts a simple wedge or arrow shape pointing inward, showing the direction of entering.

example.hanzi: 运动员们进入了体育场。
example.pinyin: Yùndòngyuánmen jìnrù le tǐyùchǎng.
example.english: The athletes entered the stadium.
example.fact: 进 and 入 both independently mean "to enter" — 进入 doubles up two synonymous verbs into one word, though 入 alone now reads as more literary or technical (as in 入口 "entrance," 收入 "income") while 进 alone is the everyday, spoken version.

components.note: Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'
多 (more/many) — 够 relates to having a sufficient amount
句 (jù) gives a loose sound connection to 够's reading gòu

example.hanzi: 我们一定能够解决这个问题。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yídìng nénggòu jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: We will definitely be able to solve this problem.
example.fact: 能够 is essentially a more formal, slightly emphatic version of the plain modal verb 能 ("can, to be able to") — the two are largely interchangeable, but 能够 shows up more in writing and formal speech, while bare 能 dominates everyday conversation.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 事实上,他根本不知道这件事。
example.pinyin: Shìshíshàng, tā gēnběn bù zhīdào zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: In fact, he didn't know about this at all.
example.fact: 事实上 is built from 事实 ("fact," also in this batch at rank 340) plus the locative suffix 上 ("on, in terms of") — the same 上 productively turns other abstract nouns into "in terms of X" adverbials, as in 理论上 ("theoretically") and 基本上 ("basically").

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — relates to 完's meaning 'complete, finish,' as in a fully built house.
元 (yuán) was the phonetic base; the pronunciation later shifted to wán, so only a partial rhyme remains today.

example.hanzi: 他终于完成了这项任务。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú wánchéng le zhè xiàng rènwu.
example.english: He finally completed this task.
example.fact: 完 by itself is one of Mandarin's most common resultative verb complements, tacked onto other verbs to mean "finish doing X" (吃完 "finish eating," 做完 "finish doing") — 完成 is the separate, full verb for "to complete" a formal task or project, and the two are not interchangeable despite sharing a character.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — 昨 relates to a day, specifically the one before today.
乍 (zhà) is only distantly related in sound to zuó — the connection has drifted apart over time.
日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'

example.hanzi: 昨晚我做了一个奇怪的梦。
example.pinyin: Zuówǎn wǒ zuò le yí gè qíguài de mèng.
example.english: Last night I had a strange dream.
example.fact: 昨晚 follows a simple, productive template — [day-word] + 晚 ("evening") — shared by 今晚 ("tonight") and 明晚 ("tomorrow night") — so once 昨/今/明 (yesterday/today/tomorrow) are known, all three time words come for free.

components.note: 矢 (arrow) — 医 originally related to treating arrow wounds, the root of its meaning 'to cure, doctor'
匸 gives a loose sound connection to 医's reading yī
阝 (a mound/enclosure) — relates to 院's meaning 'courtyard, institution,' an enclosed place.
完 (wán) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from yuàn.

example.hanzi: 我奶奶昨天住进了医院。
example.pinyin: Wǒ nǎinai zuótiān zhù jìn le yīyuàn.
example.english: My grandmother was admitted to the hospital yesterday.
example.fact: 院 (literally "courtyard") is a common suffix for buildings organized as an institution — the same 院 appears in 学院 ("college"), 电影院 ("cinema"), and 法院 ("court") — so recognizing the "courtyard/institution" suffix helps guess the meaning of many other buildings.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 这个办法不行,我们再想想。
example.pinyin: Zhège bànfǎ bùxíng, wǒmen zài xiǎngxiang.
example.english: This method won't work, let's think again.
example.fact: Beyond a plain refusal ("no good, won't do"), 不行 doubles as a common colloquial intensifier attached after 得 to mean "extremely" (累得不行, "exhausted beyond belief") — a dramatic stand-in for "extremely" in that same grammatical slot.

example.hanzi: 我只是跟你开玩笑而已。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhǐshì gēn nǐ kāi wánxiào éryǐ.
example.english: I was just joking with you, that's all.
example.fact: 而已 always sits at the very end of a sentence and almost always partners with 只(是) earlier in the clause ("只是...而已", "it's just...that's all") — a fixed sentence-final particle rather than a word that can move around, underlining "nothing more to it."

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 桌子上面放着一本书。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàngmiàn fàngzhe yì běn shū.
example.english: There's a book placed on top of the table.
example.fact: Beyond its literal spatial sense, 上面 extends abstractly to mean "the above-mentioned" when referring back to something already said in a text (上面提到的问题, "the problem mentioned above") — the same up/down metaphor that structures how many languages talk about textual sequence.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 那座房子还是老样子。
example.pinyin: Nà zuò fángzi háishi lǎo yàngzi.
example.english: That house still looks the same as before.
example.fact: 子 in 样子 is the same light grammatical suffix seen in 孩子 (in the companion character-deck's pilot batch) — worn down from its original meaning "child" into a semantically empty ending that simply signals "this is a noun," attached here to 样 ("kind, appearance").

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
走 (to walk/run) — 趣 originally related to hurrying eagerly toward something, extending to 'interesting, of interest.'
取 (qǔ) gives a sound close to qù, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 这本书的故事很有趣。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū de gùshi hěn yǒuqù.
example.english: The story in this book is very interesting.
example.fact: 有趣 follows a common Chinese pattern where 有 ("to have") plus an abstract noun forms an adjective — literally "has interest, has fun" — the same template behind 有名 ("famous," literally "has a name") and 有用 ("useful," literally "has use").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.
糸 (thread/silk) — 系 relates to connecting or tying things together, like threads linking into a system.

example.hanzi: “对不起,我迟到了。”“没关系。”
example.pinyin: “Duìbuqǐ, wǒ chídào le.” “Méiguānxi.”
example.english: "Sorry, I'm late." "It's okay, no worries."
example.fact: 没关系 literally means "[it] doesn't have a connection, a relationship" (没 + 关系) — much like English "no worries" or "it's nothing," it downplays a problem by denying that it has any real bearing on anything, rather than directly saying "it's fine."

components.note: 十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 我的美国朋友叫杰克。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de Měiguó péngyou jiào Jiékè.
example.english: My American friend is called Jack.
example.fact: 杰克 is a phonetic transliteration of the English name "Jack," chosen primarily to approximate the sound — but as is common practice when transliterating foreign names, the characters were also picked for their agreeable meanings: 杰 ("outstanding, heroic") and 克 ("to overcome, be capable of").

components.note: 直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'

example.hanzi: “我明天要结婚了。”“真的吗?”
example.pinyin: “Wǒ míngtiān yào jiéhūn le.” “Zhēn de ma?”
example.english: "I'm getting married tomorrow." "Really?"
example.fact: Bare 真 already works as an intensifier before an adjective (真好, "really good"), but adding 的 to make 真的 is what lets the word stand entirely on its own as an exclamation or question ("真的?!", "Really?!") — the 的 here doesn't mark possession, it just closes off the phrase so it can function independently.

components.note: 阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).
八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'

example.hanzi: 大部分学生都同意这个计划。
example.pinyin: Dà bùfen xuésheng dōu tóngyì zhège jìhuà.
example.english: The majority of students agree with this plan.
example.fact: 部分 rarely stands completely alone as a bare noun in speech — it's usually paired with a modifier like 大 (大部分, "most, the majority") or 一 (一部分, "a portion") rather than used by itself the way English "part" often is.

components.note: 女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.hanzi: 老师对学生的要求很严格。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī duì xuésheng de yāoqiú hěn yángé.
example.english: The teacher's requirements for students are very strict.
example.fact: Like 工作 in the companion character-deck's pilot batch, 要求 works as both a verb ("to demand, request") and a noun ("a requirement, demand") with no change in form — Chinese frequently lets a single word cross that verb/noun line for free.

components.note: 米 (grain, rice) — 糟 originally named the dregs left over from making rice wine.
曹 (cáo) gives a sound close to zāo, sharing the same rhyme and tone.
米 (rice) — 糕 names a food made from rice or flour, a cake.
羔 (gāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 糕.

example.hanzi: 糟糕,我把钥匙忘在家里了!
example.pinyin: Zāogāo, wǒ bǎ yàoshi wàng zài jiā lǐ le!
example.english: Oh no, I forgot my keys at home!
example.fact: Unlike many two-character words that split their meaning evenly across both syllables, 糟糕's second syllable 糕 ("cake") contributes essentially nothing to the meaning "terrible" — it's there mainly for rhythm and rhyme with 糟 ("spoiled dregs," the syllable that actually carries the negative sense).

components.note: 阝 (a mound/settlement) — represents a city or town.
余 (surplus, remainder) — the leftover waste a city produces, which must be cleared away, giving 除 its meaning 'to remove, eliminate.'
Depicts a child wrapped in swaddling, related to 子 (child); the picture-meaning has nothing to do with its modern grammatical role marking a completed action or change of state.

example.hanzi: 除了英语,他还会说法语。
example.pinyin: Chúle Yīngyǔ, tā hái huì shuō Fǎyǔ.
example.english: Besides English, he can also speak French.
example.fact: Like 所有...都... noted in the companion pilot batch, 除了 usually works as half of a two-part frame — 除了 X,(大家)都/也/还 Y — where the second clause's 都 (an exclusive "all" reading) or 也/还 (an additive "also" reading) determines whether 除了 ends up meaning "except" or "besides."

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — 容's meaning 'to contain, hold' relates to a house holding things, extended to 'appearance, to allow, tolerate.'

example.hanzi: 这个字很容易写错。
example.pinyin: Zhège zì hěn róngyì xiěcuò.
example.english: This character is easy to write incorrectly.
example.fact: 容易 and its near-synonym 简单 (also in this batch, rank 336) overlap but aren't identical — 容易 describes how easy an action is to carry out or how likely an outcome is (容易错, "easy/likely to go wrong"), while 简单 describes something's inherent lack of complexity, closer to English "simple" than "easy."

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
扌 (hand) — relates directly to 持's meaning 'to hold, maintain.'
寺 (sì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from chí.

example.hanzi: 请保持安静。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎochí ānjìng.
example.english: Please keep quiet.
example.fact: 保 (from a caretaker cradling a child, per its component breakdown) contributes "to protect, look after," while 持 (built from the hand radical 扌) contributes "to hold" — together 保持 paints a literal image of protectively holding something steady, fitting its modern sense "to maintain, keep."

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 虽然外面很冷,但是我们还是决定出去跑步。
example.pinyin: Suīrán wàimiàn hěn lěng, dànshì wǒmen háishi juédìng chūqù pǎobù.
example.english: Although it's cold outside, we still decided to go running.
example.fact: 虽然 belongs to the same family of correlative conjunction pairs as 因为...所以... (flagged in the companion pilot batch) — it almost always shows up with 但是 or 可是 in the following clause, and dropping the second half tends to sound incomplete to a native ear even though English "although" alone is often enough.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我没想到会在这里遇见你。
example.pinyin: Wǒ méi xiǎngdào huì zài zhèlǐ yùjiàn nǐ.
example.english: I didn't expect to run into you here.
example.fact: 想到 emphasizes an idea suddenly arriving in the mind — its negative form 没想到 ("didn't expect, would never have thought") is one of the most common exclamations in spoken Chinese — while its close cousin 想起 emphasizes recalling something already known, a distinction carried entirely by the verb complement (到 "arriving at" vs 起 "rising up") after 想.

components.note: 王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.
角 (horn) — 解 pictures removing a part of an animal.
牛 (ox) — together with a knife cutting between horn and ox, 解 pictures separating something into parts, giving its meaning 'to untie' or 'to explain.'

example.hanzi: 我完全理解你的感受。
example.pinyin: Wǒ wánquán lǐjiě nǐ de gǎnshòu.
example.english: I completely understand your feelings.
example.fact: 理解 leans more formal and analytical than the everyday verb 懂 ("to understand, get it") — 理解 suits comprehending a complex idea, argument, or someone's feelings, while 懂 is the blunt, all-purpose "get it" used constantly in casual speech (懂了吗?, "get it?").

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'
扌 (hand) — relates to 据's meaning 'to rely on, according to,' as if grasping evidence in hand.
居 (jū) gave the base sound; the pronunciation later shifted to jù, keeping the same final but a different tone.

example.hanzi: 警察在现场找到了重要的证据。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài xiànchǎng zhǎodào le zhòngyào de zhèngjù.
example.english: The police found important evidence at the scene.
example.fact: 证据 combines 证 ("to prove, certify," literally "speaking the correct truth") with 据 ("to rely on, a basis," literally "grasped in hand") — literally "a proven basis to rely on," which is why it's the standard word reached for in legal and investigative contexts.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 简 originally referred to bamboo strips used for writing
间 (jiān) gives a sound close to 简's reading jiǎn, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 这个游戏的规则很简单。
example.pinyin: Zhège yóuxì de guīzé hěn jiǎndān.
example.english: The rules of this game are very simple.
example.fact: 简 originally named the bamboo strips ancient Chinese texts were written on (per its component breakdown) — one plausible account links 简's later sense of "simple, terse" to writing brief enough to fit on just a few such strips, though like many bamboo-radical etymologies this connection is more suggestive than certain.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'

example.hanzi: 每个人的看法都不同。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén de kànfǎ dōu bùtóng.
example.english: Everyone's views are different.
example.fact: 不同 and 不一样 (built by simply negating 一样, "same," from the companion pilot batch) both mean "different," but they tend to divide labor: 不同 reads more formal and comfortably modifies a noun directly (不同的意见, "differing opinions"), while 不一样 feels more colloquial and usually sits after the subject as a predicate (这两个不一样, "these two are different").

components.note: 大 (a grown man) — the figure being depicted.
一 (a hairpin) — worn across the top of the head to mark a coming-of-age ceremony, giving 夫 its meaning 'man, husband.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 王夫人今天没有来开会。
example.pinyin: Wáng fūren jīntiān méiyǒu lái kāihuì.
example.english: Mrs. Wang didn't come to the meeting today.
example.fact: 夫人 mirrors 先生 (in the companion pilot batch) as a formal title attached after a surname — but it's normally used to address or refer to someone else's wife respectfully; calling one's own wife 夫人 in casual conversation sounds stiff or old-fashioned to modern ears.

components.note: 乂 depicts a hand gripping a tool.
八 here depicts a hand-axe — a father shown wielding a tool to provide for and protect the family gave 父 its meaning 'father.'
母 depicts a kneeling woman with two dots marking breasts — an image emphasizing nursing and motherhood, giving 母 its meaning 'mother.'

example.hanzi: 我父母住在乡下。
example.pinyin: Wǒ fùmǔ zhù zài xiāngxià.
example.english: My parents live in the countryside.
example.fact: 父 and 母 are old, classical single-syllable words for "father" and "mother," but in modern everyday speech they've mostly been displaced by the colloquial doubled forms 爸爸 and 妈妈 — 父 and 母 now survive mainly inside formal compounds like 父母, 父亲, 母亲, and 祖父母 ("grandparents").

example.hanzi: 事实证明他是对的。
example.pinyin: Shìshí zhèngmíng tā shì duì de.
example.english: Facts proved that he was right.
example.fact: 事实 narrows down 事 ("matter, affair" — the same root behind 事情 in the companion pilot batch) with 实 ("real, solid, true"), giving a word that specifically stresses factuality, where plain 事情 just means "a matter" without any claim about whether it's true.

components.note: A simplified pictograph of a bird's wings spread in flight — the source of 飞's meaning 'to fly.'
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 我们的飞机明天早上起飞。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de fēijī míngtiān zǎoshang qǐfēi.
example.english: Our plane takes off tomorrow morning.
example.fact: 飞机 is a transparent modern coinage — literally "flying machine" — built from the same productive 机 ("machine") suffix found in 手机 ("cellphone," literally "hand machine") and 洗衣机 ("washing machine"), a go-to pattern whenever Chinese needed a word for a new mechanical invention.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
广 depicts a roofed building or shelter.
廷 depicts an open court or hall — together with the shelter above, giving 庭 its meaning 'courtyard, hall.'

example.hanzi: 这是一个幸福的家庭。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè xìngfú de jiātíng.
example.english: This is a happy family.
example.fact: Plain 家 is the all-purpose, everyday word for "home" or "family" (我家, "my home/family"), while 家庭 reads more formal and abstract, treating the family as a social unit — the kind of word that shows up in phrases like 家庭教育 ("family education") rather than in casual talk about one's own household.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — an older sense of 秘 was linked to grain kept out of sight, before it narrowed to 'secret.'
必 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 秘.
宓 depicts stillness and quiet beneath a roof.
山 (mountain) — a quiet, secluded mountain gave 密 its meaning 'dense, secret, close.'

example.hanzi: 这是我们两个人之间的秘密。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒmen liǎng gè rén zhī jiān de mìmì.
example.english: This is a secret between the two of us.
example.fact: 秘 and 密 both independently carry a "hidden, concealed" sense — 秘密 reinforces two already near-synonymous roots into one noun, the same word-building strategy seen elsewhere in this deck in words like 声音. As a side note, 秘 is also read bì in the surname 祕/秘, an uncommon reading unrelated to its ordinary "secret" sense.

components.note: 尸 is traditionally read as a picture of a person collapsed or bent over — the origin of its meaning 'corpse.'

example.hanzi: 警方在河边发现了一具尸体。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zài hébiān fāxiàn le yí jù shītǐ.
example.english: The police discovered a corpse by the riverside.
example.fact: 尸体 is the neutral, clinical word for "corpse," common in news and forensic contexts — Chinese also has the more respectful, softened 遗体 ("the remains") for contexts where dignity toward the deceased matters, a register split similar to English choosing between "corpse," "body," and "remains."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.hanzi: 请帮我打开窗户。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bāng wǒ dǎkāi chuānghu.
example.english: Please help me open the window.
example.fact: The 打 in 打开 has drifted far from its core meaning "to hit" — it functions here as a semantically bleached "light verb" that simply sets 开 ("open") into motion, the same bleached role 打 plays in 打电话 ("to make a phone call"), 打扫 ("to sweep, clean"), and 打算 ("to plan"), making 打 one of Mandarin's most overloaded verbs.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 检 originally related to a wooden tally or label used for checking records
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 检's reading jiǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 医生给我做了全面的检查。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng gěi wǒ zuò le quánmiàn de jiǎnchá.
example.english: The doctor gave me a thorough examination.
example.fact: 检查 is the general, everyday word for looking something over — checking homework (检查作业) or a body (体检 is short for 身体检查) — while its more technical cousins 检验 and 检测 are reserved for laboratory testing or formal quality inspection, a specificity gradient among near-synonyms.

components.note: 日 (sun) — represents the sun.
十 depicts the first rays of sunlight appearing low on the horizon — together with 日 (sun) giving 早 its meaning 'early, morning.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上七点起床。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qī diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I get up at seven every morning.
example.fact: Chinese splits "morning" three ways where English has one word: 早上 (colloquial, roughly dawn to mid-morning), 早晨 (close to 早上 but slightly more literary), and 上午 ("forenoon," extending all the way to noon and used in more neutral or formal contexts) — worth knowing which one native speakers actually reach for at a given hour.

components.note: 王 (jade, written without its dot) — 玩 originally meant to handle and admire a piece of jade, extending to 'to play, to have fun.'
元 (yuán) gives a sound distantly related to wán, having drifted apart over time.
夭 (a person leaning back) — the pose of someone laughing.
⺮ (bamboo-like strokes) — suggesting a wide grin, giving 笑 its meaning 'to laugh, smile.'

example.hanzi: 别开这种玩笑,一点都不好笑。
example.pinyin: Bié kāi zhè zhǒng wánxiào, yìdiǎn dōu bù hǎoxiào.
example.english: Don't make this kind of joke, it's not funny at all.
example.fact: 玩笑 rarely stands as the object of a generic verb like "to make" — it almost always locks into the fixed collocation 开玩笑 ("to crack a joke," literally "to open a joke"), the same way English speakers reach for "crack" specifically before "a joke" rather than a general-purpose verb.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 老师给我们布置了一项新任务。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī gěi wǒmen bùzhì le yí xiàng xīn rènwu.
example.english: The teacher assigned us a new task.
example.fact: 任务 carries a note of formal assignment — a task or mission handed down by someone in authority or an organization (军事任务 "military mission," 学习任务 "study assignment") — distinguishing it from the more neutral, everyday 事情 ("matter, thing to do") used for whatever's simply on one's plate.

meanings: the scene (of a crime, accident etc)

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'
土 (earth) — 场 relates to a flat open area of ground, such as a field or venue.
昜 (yáng) gives a hint of the sound — 场 is pronounced chǎng, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 事故现场已经被警察封锁了。
example.pinyin: Shìgù xiànchǎng yǐjīng bèi jǐngchá fēngsuǒ le.
example.english: The accident scene has already been sealed off by the police.
example.fact: 现场 combines 现 ("present, now" — the same root behind 现在 in the companion pilot batch) with 场 ("a site, venue"), literally "the present site" — a word that carries both a spatial sense (the physical scene of an event) and a temporal-immediacy sense, as in 现场直播 ("live broadcast").
